newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin gets mixed reviews year after re-election.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin gets mixed reviews year after re-election.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, who defied the odds to secure re-election exactly a year ago, wasted little time celebrating on Thursday and left others to assess the results of a difficult year.
Yeltsin, 66, began the day having talks with visiting President Haydar Aliyev of Azerbaijan and made no immediate comment on the first 12 months of his four-year, second term.

Yeltsin's allies gave him full marks for re-establishing his grip on power and giving new impetus to economic reforms after recovering from the health problems which threatened his life and sidelined him for months after he was re-elected.

His foes said they were glad he was well again, and some even singled out a few achievements for praise. But others said he had not carried out any of his election promises and accused him of driving Russia down the road to ruin.
"It's total collapse," said Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov, whom Yeltsin defeated convincingly in the election run-off on July 3 a year ago.

Yeltsin has preferred this week to let the economy do the talking for him. Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin announced on Wednesday that Russia's economy had started to grow for the first time since the Soviet Union collapsed in 1991.

Russian share prices hit a record high the same day and Chernomyrdin said economic results had on the whole been positive in the last six months, a period in which Yeltsin has reshuffled his cabinet by bringing in young reformers.

"To carry out these unpopular but necessary reforms, you need precisely the character of B. Yeltsin," Interfax news agency quoted Sergei Belyayev, a senior pro-government member of parliament, as saying.

Belyayev also praised Yeltsin's foreign policy, including a an agreement improving ties with Slav neighbour Ukraine and a partnership agreement with NATO which reduced tensions over the Western defence alliance's expansion into eastern Europe.

Liberal Grigory Yavlinsky, who was eliminated in the first round of last year's election, also welcomed the deal with NATO at a recent news conference and hailed Russia's elevated role at this year's summit of the Group of Seven industrial nations.
But he is a critic of Yeltsin's economic policies and said his main achievement had been to get well.
"The president was ill for eight of the 12 months and, thank God, worked for four," he said.

Zyuganov meted out the most hostile criticism. The communists have used their position as the biggest single group in the lower house of parliament to block reform laws, despite allowing some important economic legislation to pass.
"Not one of the president's many promises to the people has been carried out," Interfax quoted Zyuganov as saying. He said the year had been full of disappointments.
Newspapers on Thursday gave Yeltsin mixed reviews.

The popoular Moskovsky Komsomolets asked "Boris Yeltsin: puppet or puppeteer?" The pro-communist Sovietskaya Rossiya, reviewing the six years since Yeltsin first became president, said "...the results get more and more regrettable each year."

Opinion polls suggest Yeltsin's popularity has sunk after rising sharply in the election campaign, when he gradually reduced Zyuganov's once huge lead by giving energetic performances across Russia and making lavish promises.
Yeltsin appears unduly concerned by the loss in popularity -- the constitution bars him from seeking a third term.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, on whom Yeltsin relied heavily when he was ill, hinted at Yeltsin's confidence when he said this week the president had granted him three weeks holiday this year. This, he said, was "astonishingly long".
